title: The Keser as pleasure and desire: two sides of connecting yourself to something
overview:
Chapter 23 explains the *Keser* in detail: how it is the intermediary between the *ma'atzil* and the *ne'etzalim*. Its inner side, the three heads of *Atik Yomin*, is the end of the Infinite and stays above; its outer side, *Arich Anpin*, is the head of the emanations. They are one level and yet two, and the *mashal* is pleasure and desire.

Every desire has a pleasure behind it, so pleasure seems to be the inner thing; but what a person does not want he does not enjoy, like the kid banging pots and pans, whose noise only he enjoys. Neither exists without the other, so they are one entity: both are you connecting yourself to something. The soul is drawn after pleasure and flees pain so completely that the early Kabbalists called pleasure its essence. It is not quite: pleasure fills the essence and draws it out, and it is what keeps every power alive, kindness, cruelty, winning and intellect alike. Only the will is needed for the pleasure in turn, and it is not known which comes first.

sections.title: The Keser in detail: the end of the ma'atzil within, the head of the ne'etzalim without
sections.summary: Chapter 23 begins to explain the *Keser* (crown) in detail: how it is the intermediary between the *ma'atzil* (the one who emanates) and the *ne'etzalim* (the emanations). Its inner side, the three heads of *Atik Yomin*, is the last level of the *ma'atzil* and stays above; its outer side is the root and head of the *ne'etzalim*.

phrases.en: and now in detail,
now to explain the details of *Keser*.
How it is an intermediary
and how it contains both the end of the *ma'atzil*, the end of the luminary, the source of the light;
that is the inner aspect of the *Keser*.
On the other hand, the *Keser* is also the root and the head, the beginning of the *ne'etzalim*, of the emanations, of the lights;
that's the external part of the *Keser*.
And like it says in *Etz Chaim*:

blocks.text:
Now chapter 23 begins to explain the idea of *Keser* (crown), the idea of *ratzon* (will, desire) and *taanug* (delight, pleasure), and how *Keser* is an intermediary between the levels before it and after it: between the *ma'atzil* (the one who emanates), the source of the light, and the *ne'etzalim* (the emanations), the lights of *Atzilus*.

The idea of *Keser* was mentioned before in general; **now in detail**. How is it an intermediary? It contains **the end of the ma'atzil, the end of the luminary, the source of the light**, the lowest level of the emanator, and that is **the inner aspect of the Keser**.

**On the other hand, the Keser is also the root and the head, the beginning of the ne'etzalim**. It is already the first of the *sefiros* (the Divine attributes) that leave the *ma'atzil*, and **that's the external part of the Keser**. These are the two aspects of *Keser* that let it be the intermediary between the *ma'atzil* and the *ne'etzalim*, and *Etz Chaim* (the Arizal's Tree of Life) explains this about the *Keser*, how it is an intermediary.

phrases.en: and it's also known, it's common knowledge

and they are not enclothed in the *ne'etzalim*, they do not descend into the *ne'etzalim*.
and this is what it means, this is what it says in the *posuk*, that G-d transcends, He is above, raised above the days of the world.
and that's why it is called *Atik Yomin*,
the one that uproots mountains,
that he's removed from the days of the world.
So all this is known, it's common knowledge

blocks.text:
It is explained in *Etz Chaim* and it is common knowledge that the *gimmel rishin* (three heads) of *Atik Yomin*, the *Keser*, *chachma* (wisdom) and *bina* (understanding) of *Atik*, which are the *pnimiyus* (inner side) of *Keser*, **are separate and they're removed and they remain above**. **They do not descend into the ne'etzalim.**

That is what the verse means when it says that G-d transcends, He is raised above **the days of the world**. The days of the world are the *middos* (emotional attributes) of *Atzilus*. The *middos* of *Atik* already relate to what goes on in the world, but the three heads of *Atik* are above that.

**That's why it is called Atik Yomin.** They usually translate *Atik Yomin* as "the Ancient of Days". But *atik* can mean three things: old or ancient, removed, and also to copy. Here it is the idea that it is removed from the days of the world, removed from the *middos*, as in **the one that uproots mountains**: **he's removed from the days of the world**.

**So all this is known**: it is common knowledge that the *pnimiyus* of *Keser* is removed from the days of the world, and that is the end of the *ma'atzil*; and the *chitzoniyus* (outer side) of *Keser* relates to the world, and that is the root and the head of the *ne'etzalim*.

As usual, the Mitteler Rebbe begins a new topic by quoting the sources about it and giving the basic kabbalistic terms of that level, and then he gives the *meshalim* (analogies) and explanations. Here he has quoted what *Etz Chaim* says about this level, and now he adds a question, almost.

sections.title: One level or two? Atik Yomin is the pleasure, Arich Anpin the desire
sections.summary: *Atik Yomin* and *Arich Anpin* are counted as one level, the *Keser*, and yet *Atik* is the end of the Infinite and *Arich* the head of the emanations. The explanation is the *mashal* of *taanug* (pleasure), which stands for *Atik*, and *ratzon* (desire), which stands for *Arich*.

phrases.en: we have to understand,
we have to understand this in a detailed way,

phrases.he: בהיות שעתיק יומין ואריך אנפין נחשב לאחד,
phrases.en: because on the one hand we see that *Atik Yomin* and *Arich Anpin* are considered one level,

phrases.he: רק שבכללות נחשב בחינת עתיק יומין מסוף עולם האין סוף,
phrases.en: but in general we consider *Atik Yomin* to be the end of the world of the *Ein Sof*, the end of the world of the infinite,

phrases.he: ובחינת אריך אנפין הוא שרש וראש לנאצלים,
phrases.en: and we consider *Arich Anpin* to be the root and the head, the beginning, for the *ne'etzalim*, for the limited worlds,
like it says in *Etz Chaim*.

blocks.text: **We have to understand this in a detailed way.** On the one hand *Atik Yomin* and *Arich Anpin* are **considered one level**: *Keser* is considered one level. **But in general we consider Atik Yomin to be the end of the world of the Ein Sof, the end of the world of the infinite, and we consider Arich Anpin to be the root and the head, the beginning, for the ne'etzalim, for the limited worlds**, as *Etz Chaim* says.

blocks.question: So is the Keser one level, or is it two levels?
blocks.text: Obviously it is both. On the one hand *Keser* is one level: *Atik* and *Arich Anpin* are really the same thing, not two different things. On the other hand there are these two aspects to it, and they are distinct: when we call it *Atik Yomin* it is removed, and when we call it *Arich Anpin* it is enclothed in the worlds. What we have to understand is how this relationship works, and now he will begin giving a *mashal* (analogy) to explain it.

phrases.en: and the explanation of these matters is known,
that the *mashal* for this is pleasure and desire.

blocks.title: Pleasure and desire
blocks.text: **The explanation of these matters is known**: **the mashal for this is pleasure and desire.** The *mashal* for *Atik Yomin* is pleasure, and the *mashal* for *Arich Anpin* is desire.

sections.title: Which is inside? Every desire has a pleasure in it, and nothing is enjoyed without being wanted
sections.summary: Since nobody would want riches or honor if they gave no pleasure, the pleasure seems to be the inner cause of the desire. But a thing a person does not want he does not enjoy at all, so the desire seems to be the inner cause of the pleasure.

phrases.he: ולהיות שאנו רואים שבכל רצון יש תענוג,
phrases.en: and being that we see that every desire has a pleasure in it, has a pleasure behind it,

phrases.he: ולולי התענוג לא היה רצון לדבר כלל
phrases.en: and if it wasn't for that pleasure, then you wouldn't want it at all.
for example the desire for riches, or the desire for honor, for glory,
if it wouldn't be that there was a pleasure,
you wouldn't want it at all.

blocks.text: We see that **every desire has a pleasure in it, has a pleasure behind it, and if it wasn't for that pleasure, then you wouldn't want it at all.** The whole reason you want a thing is that you will enjoy it when you get it. **For example the desire for riches, or the desire for honor, for glory**: if it was not fun to be rich, and it was not pleasurable to be honored, **you wouldn't want it at all**.

blocks.title: The tax form and the autographs
blocks.text: If it was only a nuisance to have a lot of money and a complicated tax form to fill out, people would not want to be rich. And if it was only a pain to be famous, with people taking pictures of you all the time and wanting your signature and stuff, and there was no pleasure behind it, people would not want it.

phrases.he: אם כן התענוג הוא בחינת פנימיות הרצון
phrases.en: if so, that means that the pleasure is the inner thing of the *ratzon*.
seemingly.

blocks.text:
**If so, that means that the pleasure is the inner thing of the ratzon**: the real thing behind the desire is pleasure. **Seemingly.** Seemingly the motivation, what gives rise to the desire, is that you can get pleasure from the thing. So the pleasure is the main thing, the inner cause, and that is why it is called the *pnimiyus*; the desire is just an expression of that pleasure, an outcome of it. First there is the pleasure, the fact that he enjoys being rich, and then comes the desire to be rich, in order to get that pleasure. First he enjoys honor, and then comes the desire for honor.

That is the way it seems. But it is not that simple. Why?

phrases.en: but however, we also see the opposite,
We see that if a person does not have a desire for something, he will not enjoy it.

phrases.he: שהרי דבר שלא ירצה בו לא יתענג ממנו
phrases.en: if a person doesn't want something, he will not delight in it, he won't enjoy it,
at all.
If so, that means that the desire is the inner thing of the *taanug*,

blocks.text: **But however, we also see the opposite**: **if a person does not have a desire for something, he will not enjoy it.** How do we see that? **If a person doesn't want something, he will not delight in it, he won't enjoy it, at all.** **If so, that means that the desire is the inner thing of the taanug**: what decides whether you enjoy something or not is whether you wanted it or not.

blocks.title: Food stuffed down the throat
blocks.text: We see that even something normally considered pleasurable is not enjoyed if a person does not want it. In *halacha* (Jewish law) there is the case of someone who stuffs food down another person's throat: he did not want to eat it, he was forced to, and he does not enjoy it. That is relevant in *halacha* because with certain things the only problem is getting *hanaa* (benefit, enjoyment) from them, and if somebody has something stuffed down his throat, there is no *hanaa*. And the same in other situations where somebody is forced to do something: he does not enjoy it.

blocks.title: The kid banging pots and pans
blocks.text: A kid banging on pots and pans. It is really noise, it is not like music, it is not a nice sound. But the one making the noise enjoys it, and everybody else hates it. He wants to make the noise, so since he wants it, he enjoys it. Everybody else does not want it, so they hate it.

blocks.title: The favorite CD
blocks.text:
Music is the opposite case: it is inherently pleasurable. But even there, if somebody does not want to listen to it, he will not enjoy it. If he is not in the mood, even if it is his favorite CD, and right now what he wants is quiet, it is painful to him. You could say that he is in a mood where it is painful, so really he does not want it because he does not enjoy it.

But even if he just decides he does not want to listen to it, he will not enjoy it. Say somebody becomes *frum* (religiously observant) and does not want to listen to non-Jewish music anymore, and someone puts it on in the room. You see a lot of times that he will be disturbed that the music is on, because he does not want to listen to it. Nothing happened that made him stop liking it, and yet he will not enjoy it. So this is the opposite: when you decide you want something, then you enjoy it.

sections.title: Neither exists without the other, so they are one: two sides of connecting yourself to something
sections.summary: Since neither desire nor pleasure exists without the other, they must be one *mahus* (entity). Both are the self connecting to something: desire while it is not yet had, pleasure once it is, and the connection itself is a third, higher thing, the *Radla*. This holds for simple and essential pleasure and desire and for the *murkav* (composite) kind alike.

phrases.en: and on the other hand, we see
that you cannot have one without the other.

phrases.he: כי אין לרצון קיום בלא תענוג ואין לתענוג קיום בלא רצון
phrases.en: You can't have a desire without a pleasure, and you can't have a pleasure without a desire.
based on this,
We must say that they are really one entity.

phrases.he: מאחר שמאמצעות חיבורם יחד דוקא יתקיים כו'
phrases.en: because they can only exist when you have them both together.

blocks.text: On the one hand we saw that the pleasure is the *pnimiyus*; on the other hand, that the *ratzon* is the *pnimiyus*. Now he says that **you cannot have one without the other**. They are interdependent: **you can't have a desire without a pleasure, and you can't have a pleasure without a desire.** So you cannot really say that one is the *pnimiyus* and stands alone, and the other only comes from it, because neither one can exist without the other. They are always in coexistence, always interdependent.

**Based on this**, **we must say that they are really one entity**, **because they can only exist when you have them both together.** If desire and pleasure were really separate things, you could have one without the other. That it is impossible shows that really they are one thing. You will never have an example of one without the other; maybe one is dominant, but you always have them together. The desire and the pleasure are two sides of the same coin.

Basically, *ratzon* and *taanug* both really mean that you are connecting yourself to something outside of yourself. When you connect yourself to something, it is revealed either as desire or as pleasure. If it is something you connect yourself to but do not have yet, or it is not totally revealed yet, then it is a *ratzon*: you are going towards it. When you get it, you get the pleasure.

But the whole reason you get the pleasure is that you want it, and the whole reason you want it is that you are going to get pleasure from it, because really they both come from a third, higher thing that connects them: the fact that you connect yourself to it.

blocks.title: It's his sound
blocks.text:
So with the kid banging on the pots and pans: he enjoys it because he wants it, meaning that he put himself into it. He decided to do it, so he is connecting himself to this sound, and now it sounds nice to him. "It sounds beautiful, 'cause it's his sound."

And sometimes the desire is not so clear and you mainly see the pleasure. A person takes pleasure in something when he feels that he connects to it, that he associates himself with it. He says, "Ah, that reminds me of myself somehow," and so he enjoys it. And that is why he wants it: because he sees a connection of himself in this thing, he is going to want to go after it.

This inner thing that connects the two, the association of himself with the thing, is what will be mentioned later as the third head. There is *Atik*, there is *Arich*, and then there is *Radla*, *Reisha d'lo isyada*, the head that is not known. That is the *pnimiyus* of *Atik*, the innermost part of *Keser*, where you connect yourself to the thing.

blocks.title: The mouth and the stomach
blocks.text:
Right now, if you do not want something, it is because you would not enjoy it so much right now. The desire to eat, for example, is greatly amplified when you are hungry, and when you are full it starts to become painful to eat. You can still want to eat: a lot of times, if you are very hungry and eat quickly, your mouth will still want more while your stomach is totally full and it hurts to eat more. Then the *taanug* gets taken away.

The truth is that this is a fight between two different desires, the desire of your mouth and the desire of your stomach. It takes a certain amount of time for your stomach to tell your mouth to stop being hungry, so if you eat quickly you will still want more for a while. Sweet things especially make you want to eat more. But that is already complicated: it is a *ratzon murkav* (a composite will), many desires, for a reason, and not the *etzem ratzon* or the *etzem taanug*, so there is a whole bunch of *sechel* (intellect) involved. That is the whole thing of *Tikun*, which was discussed already a little.

phrases.he: וכל זה בין בתענוג ורצון פשוט ועצמי,
phrases.en: And all of this applies whether you're speaking about an essential and simple pleasure and desire,
or whether you're speaking about a pleasure and desire that is *murkav*, it's complex,
that the soul is spread and drawn after it,
even though it's not something connected to yourself,
it's something separate,

blocks.text:
**All of this applies whether you're speaking about an essential and simple pleasure and desire, or whether you're speaking about a pleasure and desire that is murkav, it's complex**: based on a reason, so that you want this this much and that that much, with different priorities, a whole complicated system of desires connecting to each other and preceding each other, something separate from you.

An essential *ratzon* and *taanug* is still part of you: you desire part of yourself. That is the *chafetz chesed* (the desire for kindness) of chapter 10. The original desire is inside you: you want to be a nice person, you enjoy being nice.

The *ratzon murkav* is when it goes out of you: **the soul is spread and drawn after it, even though it's not something connected to yourself**; **it's something separate**, like money and food and stuff like that. When you want a good piece of chocolate cake or ice cream, that is a *ratzon murkav*: something separate from you that your soul is drawn after. In either case, the *ratzon* and the *taanug* are really one thing.

sections.title: The soul is drawn after pleasure and flees pain: it looks as if pleasure is its essence
sections.summary: The soul's nature is to be drawn after anything pleasurable, until its whole self is caught up in it, even in a pleasure separate from it like honor, money or winning; and it runs from pain to exactly the same degree. So the soul seems to be a *hiyuli* (raw potential) for pleasure, and the early Kabbalists declared that pleasure is its essence and nothing is higher.

phrases.en: however,

phrases.he: בכלל אנו רואים שהנפש טבעה להתמשך אחר דבר שיש בו תענוג,
phrases.en: In general, we see that the nature of the soul is that it's drawn after anything that is pleasurable,

phrases.he: עד שיכול להיות כל עצמותה נמשך ונכלל בו
phrases.en: until a person's whole self, their whole essence can get caught up in this pleasure,
when it's a *taanug murkav* in just a very specific thing that's separate from themselves,
For example, let's say honor,
Or money,
Or it could be in other things, in *chachma*,
*Hispaarus* means to show off.
and so too with any other *midda*,
or something that the soul covets, something that a person craves and desires,
like the *taava* for any of the pleasures of this world.

blocks.text: **In general, we see that the nature of the soul is that it's drawn after anything that is pleasurable, until a person's whole self, their whole essence can get caught up in this pleasure.** And this is the most powerful: even **when it's a taanug murkav in just a very specific thing that's separate from themselves**, a person can get totally obsessed, carried away and caught up with the pleasure.

**For example, let's say honor**: some people get totally caught up in wanting honor and fame, and it becomes their whole life. **Or money**: some people's whole life is that they want money. It is a separate thing from them, but the pleasure they get in it totally consumes them. **Or it could be in other things, in chachma**: the classic professor, whose whole life is his intellectual work. And in *middos*: some people are very into *chesed* (kindness), and their whole life is to be kind; for some it is *din* (judgement), they want justice; *netzach* (victory): some people are very competitive, their whole life is to win and always be one up. **Hispaarus means to show off**: some people need everybody to praise them and "ooh and ahh" at them. **And so too with any other midda**: *yesod*, say a teacher whose whole life is teaching and giving over; or *Malchus*, to be a king.

Or it is **something that the soul covets, something that a person craves and desires, like the taava** (craving) **for any of the pleasures of this world**: food, any physical thing. A person can get totally caught up in his desire for these things.

phrases.he: אף על פי שכל אלה אינן בבחינת עצמיות התענוג ההיולי,
phrases.en: even though none of these things are essential pleasures coming from the *taanug hiyuli*, from the essential *taanug*,
just that the soul is drawn after these things and it craves them, or it covets them.

phrases.he: אבל מזה נראה שעצם הנפש הוא בבחינת תענוג ההיולי
phrases.en: But from this, that the soul is drawn after anything pleasurable, we see that the soul is like a *hiyuli* for pleasure, it's like the essence of pleasure.

phrases.he: על כן תומשך אחר עונג מורכב
phrases.en: and therefore the soul will be drawn after any pleasure, even a *oneg murkav*, even something separate from it,
and it will run away from pain,
which is the opposite of pleasure.

blocks.text: **None of these things are essential pleasures coming from the taanug hiyuli, from the essential taanug**; it is **just that the soul is drawn after these things and it craves them**. **But from this, that the soul is drawn after anything pleasurable, we see that the soul is like a hiyuli for pleasure, it's like the essence of pleasure.**

**Therefore the soul will be drawn after any pleasure, even a oneg murkav, even something separate from it, and it will run away from pain, which is the opposite of pleasure.** The soul is this ability for pleasure. As will be said, it is not quite the essence of the soul, but it is almost the essence of what a human soul is: the ability to experience pleasure. That experience is like the existence of the soul. So the soul goes after anything pleasurable, because that is what it is; and pain means that the soul is being taken out of that thing, and that is why a person goes away from what is painful.

phrases.he: עד שב' קוין שקולין הן ממש
phrases.en: to the point that these are two equally weighed lines, that these two polar opposites of pleasure and pain are totally equal.

phrases.he: שכפי ערך התפשטות הנפש במלאת אורה בדברי תענוג,
phrases.en: that to the exact same extent that the soul, its light, becomes full from something that's pleasurable,

phrases.he: כן תתכווץ ותתמעט אורה בצער ויגון בתכלית כו'
phrases.en: So too with the reverse, that something that's painful can cause a person to totally remove themselves, and it diminishes the light of the soul,

blocks.text: **These are two equally weighed lines**: the two polar opposites, pleasure and pain, are totally equal. **To the exact same extent that the soul, its light, becomes full from something that's pleasurable**, when a person has pleasure, the soul expresses itself and is drawn into everything, the *sechel* and the *middos*; it puts its whole self into the thing, and that makes a big *hispashtus* (spreading forth) of the soul. **So too with the reverse**: something painful **diminishes the light of the soul**. A person in pain retracts and withdraws into himself, to the point where he will not express anything; he will not use his *sechel* or his *middos*, and everything becomes totally dry and mechanical.

That is why very painful experiences, something traumatic, can make a person withdraw and be so pained, maybe even in life in general, that his soul does not express itself anymore. On the other hand, when a person has a big pleasure, it brings out all his qualities. He is able to do everything much better, with much more life, energy and vitality, because the pleasure draws the soul into everything.
This is what *Chassidus* (Chassidic teaching) does in G-dliness: it reveals the G-dly *taanug* in everything. And that is why it brings so much more vitality into everything.

phrases.en: from this we see,
this shows us the essential nature of the soul
that it is pleasure.
and the main proof,
is the fact that the soul will run away and be withdrawn from pain.
this is more of a proof than the pleasure,

blocks.text: **From this we see**, **this shows us the essential nature of the soul**, **that it is pleasure**: the life of the soul is the idea of pleasure. **And the main proof is the fact that the soul will run away and be withdrawn from pain.** **This is more of a proof than the pleasure.** From the fact that the soul is drawn after pleasure you could say, "Well, the soul is really something else, and pleasure is just an add-on, a bonus." But that the pain takes the soul away shows that this is really what it is.

phrases.he: ועל כן גזרו אומר המקובלים הראשונים, שהתענוג נחשב מעצם הנפש,
phrases.en: And therefore, the early Kabbalists declared that pleasure is the essence of the soul.

blocks.text: **And therefore, the early Kabbalists declared that pleasure is the essence of the soul**, **and they said, there's nothing higher than pleasure.**

sections.title: But it is not so: pleasure fills the essence and draws it out, until the soul can expire
sections.summary: The Mitteler Rebbe answers that pleasure is not really the essence of the soul. The essence is higher; great pleasure fills it and draws it out, until it is almost wholly spent in the thing, as in *klos hanefesh* (the soul's expiring), and intense pain can spend it completely too.

phrases.en: and this is not true, it's not true that it's really the essence of the soul, and it's not true that it's the highest level.

phrases.he: רק שהעצמיות דנפש תתמלא מן התענוג הרב
phrases.en: Rather, the essence of the soul is really higher, but the essence of the soul is filled from great pleasure.
and it's drawn after something that's pleasurable, and it puts its whole essence into it, its whole self into it,
to the point that it will almost completely lose itself in the thing,
like it says *kalsa nafshi*,

blocks.text: **And this is not true**: **it's not true that it's really the essence of the soul, and it's not true that it's the highest level.** They did not mean it totally literally. It is the highest level that is expressed, the deepest level of the soul that is expressed. The Mitteler Rebbe is not saying that they were wrong; just that the statement is not totally a true statement. It is said relatively speaking.

**Rather, the essence of the soul is really higher, but the essence of the soul is filled from great pleasure.** Pleasure brings out the essence of the soul, and the more pleasure, the more the essence is brought out. It is drawn after something pleasurable **and it puts its whole essence into it, its whole self into it, to the point that it will almost completely lose itself in the thing, like it says kalsa nafshi** (my soul expired): the idea of *klos hanefesh*, where sometimes from a great G-dly pleasure a person will die. His soul has such pleasure that it is totally drawn after the G-dly pleasure and leaves the body.

blocks.title: Klos hanefesh comes from the revelations, not the essence
blocks.text: This only happens from the *giluyim* (revelations) of G-dliness, not from the essence of G-dliness. The *giluyim* of G-dliness are more in the higher worlds, so if the soul gets a great pleasure from them, it is drawn away from the body, up to the spiritual worlds. But the essence of G-dliness is found *davka* (precisely) in the physical world, because G-d chose to have a *dira b'tachtonim* (a dwelling below). If a person recognizes that level, it causes *shov* (return) as opposed to *ratzo* (running out): it draws the soul back down into the body, and the soul wants to be here. Then it gets this pleasure here in the world, which is actually greater, because in the physical world you can have *hasagas hamahus* (a grasp of the essence) of G-dliness, of G-d Himself. When a person does not appreciate that, he can have this *klos hanefesh*.

phrases.en: and on the other hand,
the soul can also be completely exhausted, completely burnt up, with the diminishing of the light completely,
through and through,
from intense pain,

blocks.text: **And on the other hand, the soul can also be completely exhausted, completely burnt up, with the diminishing of the light completely, through and through, from intense pain.** A person can also have *klos hanefesh* from a lot of pain. That is the idea of depression: a person loses his pleasure in life, his soul gets removed from his body, and it can even go so far that he will actually die.

blocks.title: Spouses who die one after the other
blocks.text: Sometimes it happens with a husband and wife: they are so connected to each other that if one of them dies, G-d forbid, very shortly afterwards the other one will also die. They had such a great pleasure in the person, and it is so painful to lose him, that the soul is drawn out of the body. There you see very strongly how the person's whole self is connected to this pleasure, and the pain totally takes him away.

blocks.title: The dog on the boy's grave
blocks.text: You see it even with animals. There is a story of a boy who had a dog, and they were very close. Then the boy was killed in a car accident, and a little afterwards the dog disappeared. They found the dog lying on the boy's grave: he had gone back there because it was the last place he saw him, and he was just lying there. The dog's whole pleasure was his boy, and when he lost him, his whole life was taken away.
And you see the other side too: if somebody has a great pleasure in something, he will forget and drop everything else and just totally put himself into this thing.

sections.title: A clearer proof: the pleasure in each power is what keeps it alive
sections.summary: In every particular power of the soul, the pleasure in it is what keeps it existing: the kind man lives from his pleasure in doing good, the cruel man from his pleasure in cruelty, the competitor from winning, until if he loses he gets sick. So too intellect: without the pleasure in it a person cannot come up with any *chachma*, and the moisture over the brain, the *hiyuli* of pleasure, is the source of all intellect and makes the wise man's face shine.

phrases.he: וראיה ברורה יותר ממה שאנו רואים שגם בפרטי כחות של הנפש, הנה בחינת העונג שבזה הכח בפרטות, הוא עיקר קיום מציאותו תמיד
phrases.en: And even a clearer proof for this is that we see that even with each of the individual powers of the soul, the pleasure in this power is the main thing that keeps it going, that gives it its strength.
for example, the attribute of kindness,

phrases.he: גם שהוא עצמי וטבעי בטבע הטוב להטיב,
phrases.en: even though we say that it's an essential part of a person's nature that he's a nice person,
the main thing that maintains this *midda*, this nature, is the pleasure
that he derives a great pleasure from giving, bestowing goodness.
and this is really what maintains this nature.

phrases.he: שהוא מה שטבעו להתענג ביותר מן ההטבה,
phrases.en: that his nature is to derive a lot of pleasure from bestowing goodness,

phrases.he: עד שכל עיקר חיותו בנפשו בא על ידי עונג זה
phrases.en: to the point that the main vitality of his soul, his whole life, comes through this pleasure
of goodness and kindness.

blocks.text: **And even a clearer proof for this is that we see that even with each of the individual powers of the soul, the pleasure in this power is the main thing that keeps it going, that gives it its strength.** **For example, the attribute of kindness**: **even though we say that it's an essential part of a person's nature that he's a nice person**, if we examine what it means that his nature is to be nice, **the main thing that maintains this midda, this nature, is the pleasure**, **that he derives a great pleasure from giving, bestowing goodness.**

**This is really what maintains this nature.** That is what it really means that he is a nice person: he derives a lot of pleasure from doing nice things, and therefore he wants to do them all the time. **His nature is to derive a lot of pleasure from bestowing goodness, to the point that the main vitality of his soul, his whole life, comes through this pleasure of goodness and kindness.** That is his whole life.

This does not mean that he does not really want to do the kindness and just wants the pleasure. His pleasure is really in doing the kindness, in helping the other person. He is not looking to help himself; his pleasure is when the other person is helped. What it means is that he associates himself with kindness. That is who he is, and his whole vitality, his whole self, his whole ego ("not in a negative sense of ego, but his whole being"), his whole sense of self, comes through kindness.

So the more kindness he does, the more pleasure it gives him, because that validates and expresses his self: he sees himself as a nice person, so the more kindness he does, the more he is seeing himself. And again: here his sense of self is that he is selfless. That is his whole being, so it does not take away from the selflessness of his kindness. His whole identity is that he gives from himself to others. This is not someone who really just wants people to praise him and look at him as great and does kindness for that. He really wants the kindness.

phrases.en: and on the other side,
somebody that's naturally cruel,

phrases.he: אין זה רק שזהו כל חיותו בתענוג זה שעושה רע ואכזריות, כידוע

blocks.text: **And on the other side, somebody that's naturally cruel**: what does it mean? That inflicting pain on somebody makes him feel great. He enjoys it, it makes him feel big, and the more cruelty he can impose on people, or animals or whatever, the happier he is.

phrases.en: the same thing with the attribute of competitiveness, conquering, that he wants to win.

phrases.he: כל עיקר קיומו רק העונג המופלג,
phrases.en: What makes a person want to be competitive and to win is that he gets a great pleasure from winning.

phrases.he: עד שחיות נפשו נמשך כולה בזה
phrases.en: until his whole vitality of his soul is drawn into this.
that he beats the other person.
and if he will not win,
then he'll get sick,

blocks.text: **The same thing with the attribute of competitiveness, conquering, that he wants to win.** **What makes a person want to be competitive and to win is that he gets a great pleasure from winning.** Somebody who does not associate himself so much with being a winner will not get such a pleasure from it. But somebody who is very into winning sees that as his whole self: it makes him significant, it makes him who he is, that he can win and beat other people. So he gets a great pleasure from it, and if he cannot do it he will be very pained. **Until his whole vitality of his soul is drawn into this**: this is his whole life, the way he feels special, all from being able to win, **that he beats the other person**.
**And if he will not win, then he'll get sick.** He is so caught up in competition that he has to win, and if he does not win he will be so disturbed that he will get sick from it.

I think you see this with a lot of world champions. Some of them are good sports; they enjoy the game. But some of them, apparently, like Bobby Fischer with winning chess, were like that. It was his whole self, his whole ego, to win and to crush the other person, and he would do it viciously; he would even get sick over it.

sensitivity.reason: Names Bobby Fischer, a public figure who died in 2008, and describes him as vicious and sick over losing.
sensitivity.publishable: I think you see this with a lot of world champions. Some of them are good sports; they enjoy the game. But for some of them winning is their whole self, their whole ego: to win and to crush the other person, so much that they would even get sick over losing.

phrases.he: וכך הוא בכל פרטי פרטי המדות
phrases.en: and so it is with all of the little minute details of the *middos*, all the individual *middos*,
even including *chachma* and *ratzon*, even intellect and desire.
the main thing that keeps them, that maintains them, the main maintaining force and their main source is the pleasure that a person gets in this.
and if it wouldn't be for the pleasure a person derived from intellect, from getting an understanding of something, or arriving at a new idea,

phrases.he: אין לו כח לחדש שום חכמה,
phrases.en: he would not be able to originate any sort of *chachma*,
like we see tangibly,

blocks.text: **And so it is with all of the little minute details of the middos, all the individual middos, even including chachma and ratzon, even intellect and desire**: **the main maintaining force and their main source is the pleasure that a person gets in this.** **If it wouldn't be for the pleasure a person derived from intellect, from getting an understanding of something, or arriving at a new idea, he would not be able to originate any sort of chachma, like we see tangibly.**

phrases.en: like it says in the *Gemara*,
if it wouldn't be for the joy of study, then I would not be able to learn so well.

blocks.text: **Like it says in the Gemara**, one of the sages of the *Talmud* said it: **if it wouldn't be for the joy of study, then I would not be able to learn so well.**

It is not a matter of being disciplined. You can force yourself to do something, but to actually be good at something and accomplish, you have to be invested in it. The truth is that forcing yourself does help, because it comes from your *koach haratzon* (power of will), which is really the same thing as *taanug*. Making yourself do it means that you invest yourself in it, you connect yourself to it, and the effort you put in will give you a pleasure in it. But that is not what this is about.

Right now the point is straight: if a person does not have the pleasure, he is not going to be good at it. When a person does not enjoy a certain subject, his mind is basically off. He is not really there; he is just hearing the words, not really thinking about it, so he will not understand well or come up with new ideas. But a person who really enjoys it puts his whole mind into it, thinks about it deeply and really gets a feel for the idea, an intimate knowledge of it, and is able to understand it properly and come up with ideas.

phrases.he: וכידוע בענין חכמת אדם תאיר פניו,
phrases.en: and as is known, the idea that it says that the wisdom of a person enlightens his face,
because the liquid, the liquid that's over the brain,
this liquid is physically the *hiyuli* of *taanug*, it's the essence of pleasure.

phrases.he: הוא המקור להשכיל כל שכל כו'
phrases.en: And that liquid is also the source of *sechel*, of intellect,

blocks.text: **As is known, the idea that it says that the wisdom of a person enlightens his face**: when a person gets a *chachma*, an idea, his face shines, and somebody who is a *chacham b'etzem* (wise in essence) has a face that is always shining. Why? **Because the liquid, the liquid that's over the brain**, between the skull and the brain: **this liquid is physically the hiyuli of taanug, it's the essence of pleasure. And that liquid is also the source of sechel, of intellect**, what is called the *koach hamaskil* (the power of insight).

There are membranes over the brain, and when this liquid is filtered through them, depending on how it is filtered, it activates *sechel* (more about how this works later). The point is that when this liquid hits the brain it both triggers the thought process of the brain and gives pleasure. So really, what the intellect is, is a localized and specific pleasure, a pleasure in a certain form; that is the idea of this *chachma*. And that pleasure comes out as a shining of the face: it increases the blood flow of the face, so it shines.

When you see a person very happy or very excited, his face shines. Like when you drink, your face gets red: there is a color in the face. Depending on what kind of pleasure, there are different colors. So somebody very wise has a certain glow to his face from this pleasure. And the same with somebody very kind: he is always happy, he has a certain glow, because he enjoys life. Even the painful parts he enjoys.

sections.title: Only the will is needed for the pleasure: the two are one essence, and it is not known which comes first
sections.summary: Pleasure keeps every power going, but only the will is also needed for pleasure: without wanting it, a person does not enjoy kindness, study, winning, money or honor. Both are the whole soul drawn after a thing, so whatever opposes the will is painful and whatever is enjoyed is wanted; they are one *mahus*, sometimes one inner and sometimes the other, never one without the other, whether simple or *murkav*.

phrases.en: however,

phrases.he: ברצון בלבד אנו רואים שבלא רצון אין תענוג
phrases.en: unique is *ratzon* among all of the *kochos* of the *nefesh*, that only with *ratzon* do we see that without *ratzon* there will be no *taanug*.
and this we see even with all the *pratei middos*,

blocks.text: **However**, **unique is ratzon among all of the kochos of the nefesh** (the powers of the soul), **that only with ratzon do we see that without ratzon there will be no taanug.** You cannot say that without *chachma* there will be no *taanug*. On the one hand the *taanug* is the source that keeps all the powers going; but only with *ratzon* is the *ratzon* also the source of the *taanug*, so that you need the *ratzon* for the *taanug*. With everything else it goes one way only: without *chachma* you still have *taanug*.

In other words, if you do not enjoy the *chachma*, you will not have a *chachma*, and if you do not enjoy *bina*, you will not have a *bina*: you will not be able to understand, or be very good at being logical. But if you do not have the *bina* or the *chachma*, you will still have the *taanug*. It is a one-way relationship. You need the *taanug* to keep the *sechel* and the *middos* going, but you do not need the *sechel* or the *middos* to have a *taanug*. "You don't have to be smart to enjoy things." It is not that the smarter you are, the more *taanug* you will have. But with *ratzon*: if you do not want something, you will not enjoy it, as was said. **And this we see even with all the pratei middos** (the particular attributes).

phrases.he: כמו אם לא ירצה בחסד או דין אין לו בו תענוג כלל
phrases.en: if you don't want *chesed* or if you don't want *din*, you won't enjoy it.
and also if he doesn't want to study, he doesn't want to come up with ideas now,
you won't enjoy it at all.

phrases.he: וכן אם לא ירצה בניצוח כלל
phrases.en: And if a person doesn't want to win at all,
then he won't have a pleasure in winning.
And the same thing with showing off.
and the same thing with the other pleasures of this world,
like money and honor and the like,

phrases.he: בלא רצון אין תענוג בהן כלל וכלל
phrases.en: if a person doesn't want them, then he won't enjoy them at all.

blocks.text: **If you don't want chesed or if you don't want din, you won't enjoy it.** If a person wants to be nice, he will enjoy it; if he does not want to, he will not, and the same with *din*. Even somebody who normally enjoys *chesed*: if a time comes when he does not want it, say because it will be bad for him, then he will not enjoy it. **And also if he doesn't want to study, he doesn't want to come up with ideas now, you won't enjoy it at all.**

blocks.title: Playing with a little kid
blocks.text: **If a person doesn't want to win at all, then he won't have a pleasure in winning.** Say you are playing with a little kid and you want him to win. You will not enjoy it if you win, because you do not want to: you want him to win. **And the same thing with showing off.** If you want to show off and want people to make a big deal about you, you enjoy it. But if you want to keep things quiet and do not want people making a big deal about you, you will not enjoy it; it will make you uncomfortable.

**And the same thing with the other pleasures of this world, like money and honor and the like**: **if a person doesn't want them, then he won't enjoy them at all.** A person who does not want money will not enjoy having money. "What do I need it for? It's a headache." And the same with honor.

phrases.he: והיינו מפני שכללות ענין זה הוא בהיות שכל עיקר עצם הנפש נמשך אחר התענוג והרצון,
phrases.en: And this is because the general idea is that with all the *middos* it's really one thing, that the *etzem hanefesh* goes after *taanug* and *ratzon*.

phrases.he: (שהרצון הוא גם כן המשכת כל הנפש
phrases.en: that *ratzon* is also the idea of drawing your whole soul into something.

phrases.he: עד שכולה תכלה ברצון לדבר מה כו׳ כידוע)
phrases.en: To the point where a person can be totally obsessed with the *ratzon* for something.

phrases.he: על כן גם בכל פרטי כחותיה,
phrases.en: and therefore also with every one of the soul's powers,
their main existence or continuance comes from the pleasure and the desire.

blocks.text: **And this is because the general idea is that with all the middos it's really one thing, that the etzem hanefesh** (the essence of the soul) **goes after taanug and ratzon.** If you have a *taanug* and *ratzon* in something, you put yourself into that thing; if you do not, you have no pleasure in it. For **ratzon is also the idea of drawing your whole soul into something**, **to the point where a person can be totally obsessed with the ratzon for something**: his whole self can get absorbed in it.

That is basically what *taanug* and *ratzon* mean: that you connect yourself to something, you invest yourself in it. The more *taanug* and *ratzon* you have, the more you will succeed and the more you will express yourself in that thing. That is what was said, that it fills the light of the soul: the soul spreads more into the thing. And that is why they say it is like the *etzem hanefesh*. *Taanug* and *ratzon* are not the *etzem hanefesh* itself; they are what connects the *etzem hanefesh* to something else. They are two sides of the same coin. The only difference is that *ratzon* is when you are going out to something, and *taanug* is when that thing comes back to you, what you get from it.

*Ratzon* is the expression of you wanting to go and connect yourself to something: your connection to the thing is expressed as a void, so you rush to fill in the form you chose. When you have reached it, got what you wanted and filled that form, you get the pleasure, in which you feel yourself. Pleasure means that you feel yourself in this thing: "Ah, it expresses me." **And therefore also with every one of the soul's powers, their main existence or continuance comes from the pleasure and the desire.**

phrases.en: And when the *taanug* and *ratzon* are missing in something, then this thing is painful.
the opposite of pleasure.
something that opposes a person's desire,
even if it's not essentially painful,
he'll automatically be very pained.

blocks.text: **When the taanug and ratzon are missing in something, then this thing is painful**, **the opposite of pleasure.** And **something that opposes a person's desire, even if it's not essentially painful, he'll automatically be very pained.**

blocks.title: The friend who stops you in a rush
blocks.text: Say you are in a rush to go somewhere. It is not a meeting you are going to miss; you are just really excited to do something and want to do it very quickly. And somebody stops you, even your friend, and wants to talk to you for a minute. Talking to him is not a painful thing; you enjoy talking to him. But right now you do not want to, and he is stopping you from getting what you want, delaying you, so it is very painful. You are eaten up. It is automatically painful because it is stopping what you want.

phrases.he: כמו אם ירצה לאהוב שונאו, יתענג ממנו
phrases.en: For example, if a person wants to love his enemy, he'll take pleasure in him.
or if somebody doesn't want his beloved,
then he'll get pain from him.

phrases.he: וכן אם יתענג בשנאוי לו המזיקו, ירצה בו,
phrases.en: Similarly, we see with pleasure that if a person enjoys something, even if it's something that's hateful to him, that hurts him, he'll want it.

phrases.he: ואם יצטער באהוב לו, לא ירצה
phrases.en: and if a person gets pain from something that's beloved to him, something that he likes, he won't want it.

blocks.text: **For example, if a person wants to love his enemy, he'll take pleasure in him.** **Or if somebody doesn't want his beloved**, **then he'll get pain from him.** If for some reason a person wants his enemy for something, he will enjoy being with him. And if a person does not want to be with somebody, even somebody he likes, as in the example of the friend who stops you when you want to go do something, he will get pain from it.

Similarly, **if a person enjoys something, even if it's something that's hateful to him, that hurts him, he'll want it.** If somebody finds some sort of pleasure in something that is really bad for him, he will still want it. We see people develop a pleasure in drinking alcohol, or in drugs. At first it tastes bad, it is a disgusting thing, and it totally messes you up; but because some pleasure comes from it, you want it.

blocks.title: Donating blood
blocks.text: **And if a person gets pain from something that's beloved to him, something that he likes, he won't want it.** Say somebody very kind wants to donate blood, but it hurts; or it does not necessarily hurt, but when he did it, it made him faint a little. Because of the pain he does not want to do it anymore. It makes him kind of afraid to do it.

phrases.he: כי מהות אחד הן הרצון והתענוג,
phrases.en: because the *ratzon* and *taanug* are really one thing.
It's not that we don't know, it's not known. In other words, it's impossible to know which one came first.
And sometimes one is internal, the other one is external.
and sometimes you see the other way around.
but you'll never find one without the other.
If there's no pleasure, there's no desire,
and if there's no desire, there's no pleasure.
Whether it's a simple desire and pleasure, or whether it's a *murkav*, a complex desire and pleasure, meaning something separate from yourself,
like we said before,
And that is enough for the understanding.

blocks.text: **Because the ratzon and taanug are really one thing**: it is just that you are connecting yourself to something. **It's not that we don't know, it's not known. In other words, it's impossible to know which one came first.** **And sometimes one is internal, the other one is external**: sometimes one is manifest and the other is the hidden cause, **and sometimes you see the other way around**. Sometimes it looks like the *ratzon* is the *chitzoniyus* and the *taanug* the *pnimiyus*, and sometimes like the *taanug* is the *chitzoniyus* and the *ratzon* the *pnimiyus*.

**But you'll never find one without the other. If there's no pleasure, there's no desire, and if there's no desire, there's no pleasure**, **whether it's a simple desire and pleasure, or whether it's a murkav, a complex desire and pleasure, meaning something separate from yourself, like we said before.** That is the basic thing: they are really two sides of one coin, and both are really just an expression of you connecting yourself with something. **And that is enough for the understanding.** The *nimshal* (what the analogy stands for) will be explained in the next chapter.

reviewQuestions.question: How is the *Keser* an intermediary, and which of its two sides is the end of the *ma'atzil* and which the head of the *ne'etzalim*?
What can the word *atik* mean, and in what sense are the three heads of *Atik Yomin* removed from "the days of the world"?
What do the food stuffed down someone's throat, the kid banging pots and pans and the favorite CD show about desire and pleasure?
Why must desire and pleasure be one entity, and what is the third, higher thing they both come from?
Why is the soul's running away from pain more of a proof than its being drawn after pleasure?
What is unique about *ratzon* among the powers of the soul, compared with *chachma* and *bina*?

notes.text: The second class opens in the middle of a point ("Yeah, I mean right now if you don't want it, because you wouldn't enjoy it so much right now", 02 w0-18), as if answering a question that is not on the tape. It continues the first class's discussion of desire and pleasure and is placed, with outOfPlace, under lines 13-14 as the mashal of the mouth and the stomach.

A few remarks in the fourth class sound like answers to a listener who is not heard: "Well, it's not a matter of being disciplined" (04 w169), "Like when you drink, your face gets red. Yeah, that's what I mean" (04 w708-720), "No, you don't have to be smart to enjoy things. Right?" (04 w1021-1031). They are written as his own points, not as student questions.
At 01 w881-892 the transcript has "Now the Maggid will begin giving a mashal"; it is presumably a slip, or the machine's hearing, for the Mitteler Rebbe. The block says "he".

Phrases read without English: line 17's "ומדות בחסד ודין וניצוח" (he explains each with examples instead), line 18's closing "וכהאי גוונא", line 28's "כידוע" and line 32's "אין זה רק ... כידוע" (he explains it as "what does it mean..."). Line 33's second phrase cites his explanation right after the reading (03 w1620-1639), "what makes a person want to be competitive and to win is that he gets a great pleasure from winning", his only rendering of it. Line 50's second phrase cites his correction of himself ("It's not that we don't know, it's not known"). Line 1's second phrase cites "now to explain the details of Keser" (01 w87-94), his rendering of בפרטיות בחינת הכתר after a word about the Keser having been mentioned in general before; the leading "but" is dropped.

Not checked; reported as said. He reads line 3's ראשין as "rishin", spelled so in the file (gimmel rishin).

Sensitivity: one flag, the remark about Bobby Fischer as a champion who would crush opponents viciously and get sick over losing (named-person; he died in 2008). Left unflagged: the remarks that depression and grief can make a person die (03 w669-823) and that trauma makes a person withdraw (02 w1405-1451), which are observations rather than advice; and the newly frum man who no longer wants to hear non-Jewish music (01 w1769-1885), which disparages no one. A reviewer checked these again for the public edition and left them unflagged: the depression passage states that pain can take away a person's pleasure in life, as the line's klos hanefesh from pain, and gives no advice; the remark that people come to enjoy alcohol or drugs although they are bad for them (04 w2247-2295) is likewise an observation. The Bobby Fischer remark stays flagged with its publishable text.
